projects.headline: On the Digilent Nexys A7-100T (xc7a100tcsg324-1) with Vivado 2026.1, 5 of 5 requests written in plain English were answered from captures on the board, and every answer matched the known result and the value read back over the board's serial link.

projects.one_line: Ask for a capture in words: the flow picks the signals by their RTL names, sets the trigger, builds an on-chip logic analyser, captures on the board and answers in plain words, quoting only the capture.

approvals: The owner asked for this capability, set the order (front end first) and the safety rules: board memory only, power and temperature limits, design checks never skipped. No approval was needed per run.
gates: The plan matched its schema and the free tier's limits before any build.
The build passed every check of the normal flow, including timing and the debug hub's clock crossing.
The build ID read back over JTAG matched before arming (d2b75378).
Every number in the answer was checked against the capture.
agent.plan: Three signals resolved by RTL name to register outputs, packed into 2 of the 5 ports; trigger on the write strobe and the address byte; a 1024-sample window holding the 16 cycles before and 32 after that were asked for.
agent.request: First write 3 to COUNT. Then capture count, win_wr and the shell's ADDR byte when the shell writes the COUNT register (win_wr is 1 and addr is 0x80), 16 cycles before and 32 after. The write that triggers it puts 0x1234 in COUNT. Afterwards read COUNT back.

links: the agent asks the next question

story.how: A language model only restates the request as structured JSON. Everything after it is deterministic: each signal name is resolved against the RTL to a register output, the trigger becomes per-bit compare values, the window and the analyser's ports are sized within the free tier's limits, and the plan is shown before anything is built. The build reuses the normal Vivado flow and all its checks; the capture runs over JTAG while the board is driven over its serial link; the answer is written from facts computed from the samples, and a check refuses any number that the capture does not support.
story.problem: An on-chip logic analyser shows what a design really does on the board, but setting one up is slow: choosing signals that survive synthesis, packing them into the analyser's ports, writing the trigger, rebuilding and reading the waveform. On the free Vivado licence tier the analyser is also limited, so a request that does not fit fails late, after a long build.
results: 5 of 5 known-answer requests passed: a register write, one dimmer period, the serial sync byte on a rising edge, an OR of two edges and a request served by an existing build. One design, one run each, so no spread is stated.

5 debug builds of 418.1 to 531.8 seconds each (about 7 to 9 minutes); 1 of the 5 requests needed no new build because an earlier build already held its signals. Every build met timing (worst setup slack at least 3.06 ns) and stayed under 0.162 W.
Programming and capture took 48.3 to 64.7 seconds per request. Reading each request cost 0.00011 to 0.00027 US dollars, as the model provider reported.

The free tier allows one analyser and at most 5 probe ports with one comparator each. On the board Vivado refused to arm two OR terms on one port, so the planner now gives each OR term its own port; that build triggered correctly.
All 5 captures ran inside the recommended operating conditions: die 24.7 to 26.9 C, core supply 1.006 V, 0 alarms.
